{"id": "2:286/q08", "question": "How do the earning verbs differ in meaning?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q08/p1", "position": "Kasb and iktisāb can have the same meaning.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT: The correct linguistic view is that kasb and iktisab are synonymous; Dhu al-Rumma uses both forms for earning in one line. RAZI-FULL reporting الواحدي: Al-Wāḥidī says the language treats kasb and iktisāb as synonyms; Dhū al-Rummah's verse and Qurʾānic uses interchange them in 74:38, 6:164, 2:81, and 33:58. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting أهل اللغة: The sounder linguistic view treats kasb and iktisāb as synonyms, as several Qur'anic usages attest. SAMIN-DURR reporting الواحدي: Al-Wāḥidī says the sound linguistic view treats kasb and iktisāb as equivalent, citing Dhū al-Rummah's line that uses both forms together. ELMALILI: If kesb and iktisāb are synonymous, the contrast between benefit and liability comes from their objects; the first mā is read as commanded good and the second as forbidden evil. STUDYQURAN: The verbs for earning and perpetrating share a root and can be synonymous depending on context."}, {"id": "2:286/q08/p2", "position": "Kasb can extend beyond oneself; iktisāb is more restricted or effortful.", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT reporting بعضهم: Some say iktisab is narrower: kasb may benefit oneself or another, while iktisab is only for oneself; one can be a provider for family but not an iktisab-earner for them. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting منهم: Others distinguish them: earning may benefit oneself or another, whereas acquisition is only for oneself; Arabs say كاسب أهله but not مكتسب أهله, and a cited poem uses كاسبهم. SAMIN-DURR: Some distinguish the verbs: kasaba can mean earning for oneself or another, whereas iktasaba is narrower; Arabic says “he earns for his family” but not “he acquires his family,” and al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line uses kāsib. ELMALILI: Kesb can mean successfully attaining what one sought, while iktisāb means effort or action whether successful or not, making it broader in one respect and narrower in another; the terms may substitute for one another."}]}
{"id": "2:286/q09", "question": "How do لَهَا and عَلَيْهَا frame the deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q09/p1", "position": "The lām conveys benefit or possession; ʿalā conveys a burden or liability.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL: Good deeds belong to the person because they bring joy and are counted as property; evil deeds are burdens and debts. ALUSI-FULL: The pronoun in lahā refers to the generic soul; reward and punishment are understood by ellipsis, with good implied by the beneficial lām. {"id": "2:286/q12", "question": "Why is the prayer taught and repeated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q12/p1", "position": "The taught prayer expresses humility and seeks continued divine favor.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ: He recommends memorizing this supplication and praying it often. FARISI-HUJJA: The taught prayer can request an assured divine act, as in the prayers for judgment and fulfillment of promises and the angels' intercession for believers. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Ibn Atiyya says Muadh's practice may be a Prophetic report, or sound analogy with al-Fatiha because both contain supplication. TABRISI: A third reading means accidentally failing an obligation or unintentionally doing a forbidden act; the plea expresses humility even though such acts are not punished. RAZI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A Prophetic report calls supplication the core of worship; al-Razi states no grading. RAZI-FULL reporting المعتزلة: Their third reply is that praying against an act does not establish that God could do it, just as prayers against unjust judgment, disgrace, disobedience, or loss of deeds do not establish those outcomes as possible. RAZI-FULL: The plural prayer seeks fuller acceptance: when people’s spiritual intentions and desires converge on one request, its realization is stronger. QURTUBI-FULL: The prayer’s wording teaches people how to supplicate. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Each petition begins Rabbana to invoke God as their nurturer and reformer and to acknowledge their servitude and need; final clauses omit it because they conclude earlier petitions. ITQAN reporting كعب: Ka'b says Muhammad received four verses not given to Moses: the passage beginning لله ما في السماوات and ending al-Baqara, plus Ayat al-Kursi; Moses instead received a supplication. ITQAN: The end of al-Baqara closes with supplication. ALUSI-FULL: The passage resumes the believers' supplications after explaining the wisdom of obligation; it may also complete the narration of their utterances. ELMALILI: Elmalılı closes by praying that God grant worshippers a great share of the promised response when they understand these supplications and follow what they require. IBNASHUR-FULL: Repeating the address to God between coordinated clauses, though unnecessary, displays humility and supplication."}]}
{"id": "2:286/q13", "question": "What does تُؤَاخِذْنَا mean and why this form?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q13/p1", "position": "The plea asks God not to punish or call the speakers to account.", "reasons": "THALABI: تؤاخذنا means ‘do not punish us.’ WAHIDI-BASIT: La tuʾakhidhna means do not punish us. RAZI-FULL: “Do not take us to account” means “do not punish us.” RAZI-FULL: One explanation for the reciprocal form is that the forgetful person exposed himself to harm through his own action, making the punisher seem to assist in harming him. ALUSI-FULL: Muʾākhadha means punishment; the form fāʿala can carry the simple sense of fāʿala/afaʿala rather than reciprocal action. IBNASHUR-FULL: Muakhadha derives from taking in the sense of punishment, and the reciprocal form intensifies the plea not to punish for forgetfulness or error."}, {"id": "2:286/q13/p2", "position": "The reciprocal form pictures the sinner as contributing to his own punishment.", "reasons": "THALABI reporting أهل المعاني: Although the verb is in a reciprocal form, it describes one actor: the sinner has effectively opened a way for the punisher and thus shares in the taking to account. WAHIDI-BASIT: The reciprocal verb is used though punishment has one agent: the sinner exposes himself and opens the way through his own deed, as if helping the punisher seize him. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: Another explanation retains the reciprocal form because the sinner makes himself vulnerable to punishment through his deed, as though aiding his own injury. SAMIN-DURR: The reciprocal form is used for one action because the sinner exposes himself to punishment by his deed, as if helping the punisher act against him; it may also be a conventional reciprocal such as sāfartu. ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: An alternative takes the reciprocal form literally: God holds the sinner accountable while the sinner, having no rescuer but God, appeals to Him as though demanding release; Al-Alusi calls this unsound without strained interpretation."}]}
{"id": "2:286/q14", "question": "What does نَّسِينَا mean here?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q14/p1", "position": "Forgetting is literal absence of recollection.", "reasons": "ABDURRAZZAQ reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from the Prophet says God has excused this community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and what its members are compelled to do; no grading is given. ABDURRAZZAQ reporting قتادة: Qatāda says he was told that God has excused this community for forgetfulness and for thoughts that arise within them. TAB-FULL reporting قوم: Some held that asking not to be charged for forgetfulness or error is obedience and humility, not an actual request for pardon; al-Tabari says he will treat their view in a fuller work. TAB-FULL: The petition asks pardon for forgetting a required duty or mistakenly doing something forbidden without intending disobedience, through ignorance or error. TAB-FULL reporting ابن زيد: Ibn Zayd paraphrases the prayer as asking not to be charged for forgetting a duty or mistakenly committing a prohibition. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Qatada relays the Prophet’s statement that God has excused this community for forgetfulness and for thoughts that occur within themselves. ZAJJAJ reporting النبي: A prophetic report says this community is pardoned for forgetfulness and inward thoughts. IBNABIHATIM reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet says God has waived three things for his community: error, forgetfulness, and coercion. FARISI-HUJJA: نسينا may mean ordinary forgetfulness and أخطأنا an unintentional mistake; the prayer asks not to be punished for either, although believers know God does not punish them for these. FARISI-HUJJA reporting النبي: A transmitted Prophetic report says the community is absolved for error, forgetfulness, and what it is compelled to do; the author gives no grading. THALABI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Ibn Umar reports the Prophet saying that error, forgetfulness, and what people are coerced into have been lifted from his community. WAHIDI-BASIT: Even when religious law excuses forgetfulness, believers may still be taught to pray for pardon, as prophets and angels petition for things God will certainly grant. JISHUMI: The phrase may also ask God not to hold them accountable if they are exposed to forgetfulness. BAGHAWI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet said that error, forgetfulness, and coercion have been lifted from his community. KASHSHAF-FULL: The prayer asks that they not be taken to task for forgetfulness or error if either occurs through them. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Many scholars, including Ibn Atiyya, hold that the prayer concerns involuntary forgetfulness and unintentional error; he calls this correct. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting النبي: Qatada says he was told the Prophet stated that God excused his community for forgetfulness and error. RAZI-FULL: The first of two interpretations takes forgetfulness in its ordinary sense, as the opposite of remembering. RAZI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A Prophetic report says error, forgetfulness, and coercion have been lifted from the community; al-Razi gives no grading. RAZI-FULL: If forgetting and error mean intentionally doing wrong, the commanded prayer gives grave sinners grounds to hope for pardon: God instructs believers to ask not to be punished for such sins. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: Al-Razi’s Ashʿari associates argue that the verse supports the rational possibility of obligating what cannot be done: a forgetful person cannot avoid the act, yet asks God not to punish him for it. QURTUBI-FULL: The prayer asks that sin committed through forgetfulness or error be pardoned, as in the Prophetic report that these are lifted from the community. QURTUBI-FULL reporting النبي: The Prophet said that error, forgetfulness, and what people are coerced into have been lifted from his community; the author says this certainly lifts sin, while legal effects differ by case. QURTUBI-FULL: The account glosses “if we forgot” as ignorance and “or erred” as delibe

rate action, while also offering the reading of acting through forgetfulness and error. BAYDAWI-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet’s saying that error and forgetfulness have been lifted from his community supports the promised pardon. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Forgetting is absence of recollection, and forgetfulness and error are excused from accountability. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya says many scholars correctly understand the prayer as asking pardon for prevailing forgetfulness and error from the intended course. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قتادة: Qatada reports that the Prophet said God has pardoned his community for forgetfulness and error. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: One view finds here forgiveness for major sinners: the prayer would be improper if forgetfulness and error meant only unaccountable acts, so they signify deliberate sin, omission and commission respectively. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: God commands believers to ask not to be punished for sins committed in forgetfulness or error; this command supports that He grants what they request. IBNKATHIR-FULL reporting أم الدرداء: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits from Umm al-Darda that the Prophet said God overlooks three for his community: error, forgetfulness, and coercion. IBNKATHIR-FULL: Forgetfulness can mean leaving an obligation or committing a prohibition unintentionally; error means missing the sound legal form out of ignorance. IBNKATHIR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: A Prophetic report transmitted through Ibn Abbas says God lifted mistake, forgetfulness, and coercion from the community; Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban narrate it, but Ahmad and Abu Hatim faulted it. BIQAI-FULL: Forgetting means doing what was forbidden without remembering; error means doing it while remembering but without intending evil. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عمر: The Prophet said God pardons his community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and actions done under compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting عقبة بن عامر: The Prophet said God has lifted from his community mistakes, forgetfulness, and actions done under compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: The Prophet said God pardons his community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and actions done under compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting أبو ذر: The Prophet said God pardons his community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and actions done under compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting ثوبان: The Prophet said God pardons his community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and actions done under compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting أبو بكرة: The Prophet said God lifted from this community mistakes, forgetfulness, and things they are forced to do. DURR-FULL reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan transmits from the Prophet that this community is excused for errors, forgetfulness, and compulsion. DURR-FULL reporting الشعبي: Al-Shaʿbi attributes to the Prophet the report that God pardons three things: error, forgetfulness, and coercion. DURR-FULL reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan reports that God excuses a person for what he errs in, forgets, is compelled to do, or is overcome by. ALUSI-FULL reporting الطبراني: Al-Tabarani transmits a hadith that al-Nawawi grades ḥasan: the Prophet says his community is exempted for error, forgetfulness, and coercion. TABATABAI: Although the Prophet is protected from error and forgetfulness, he relies on God's protection and may ask for what he cannot secure from himself, joining the community of believers. TABATABAI: The requested forgiveness is specific to sin through error or forgetfulness, unlike the absolute “Your forgiveness, our Lord” answering the believers' absolute assent; the requests are not redundant. STUDYQURAN: Moses’ plea about forgetting recalls the believers’ prayer in 2:286 not to be taken to task for forgetting or error. STUDYQURAN reporting the Prophet: A hadith says God absolved the Prophet's community of mistakes, forgetfulness, and acts done under compulsion."}, {"id": "2:286/q14/p2", "position": "Forgetting includes abandoning or neglecting an obligation.", "reasons": "TUSTARI: A person recognizes sins by guarding the heart's light and weighing everything allowed to enter or leave it. TUSTARI: A heart occupied with what does not concern it is immediately punished by neglect of what does; only those who know God recognize this. TAB-FULL: Neglectful forgetting is a failure to perform a command; the petition seeks pardon for it, except when the neglect amounts to unbelief. Al-Tabari cites Adam’s lapse and later neglect of prayer, fasting, or memorized Quran. TAB-FULL reporting ابن زيد: Ibn Zayd says people can obey commands and leave prohibitions only through God’s mercy, and no one is saved except by it. ZAJJAJ reporting قيل: An alternative gloss takes if we forget as if we omit, and or err as committing a sin. FARISI-HUJJA: When نسي means leave, attributing it to God is figurative: people leave obedience and God leaves them without mercy or rescue; the Qurʾan also uses ترك for leaving people alone. THALABI reporting بعضهم: Another view understands forgetting as abandoning or neglecting; al-Tha'labi prefers the literal sense, though he cites 9:67 for the alternative usage. THALABI reporting ابن زيد: Ibn Zayd applies forgetting to neglecting a required duty and error to doing something forbidden. MAWARDI-FULL: Nasiya can mean deliberately neglecting God's command or simply leaving it; Qutrub cites 'they forgot God, so He forgot them' for the latter sense. WAHIDI-BASIT: Here forgetting can mean abandoning an obligation; in 9:67, people abandon God's service and are left without reward. JISHUMI reporting الحسن: Hasan supplies an omitted imperative: “and say, Our Lord.” JISHUMI: Another reading of “we forgot” is that people abandoned something because of doubt or bad interpretation, like the verse saying they forgot God and He forgot them. BAGHAWI-FULL: Another interpretation takes forgetting to mean neglecting or abandoning God, as in the verse saying they forgot God and He forgot them. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الطبري وغيره: Al-Tabari and others take forgetting as neglecting obedience and error as intentional sin; involuntary forgetfulness and error are already excused. TABRISI: One interpretation takes forgetting as abandoning obedience and error as committing sins, even deliberately; the prayer seeks forgiveness for neglected duties and wrongful acts. TABRISI: The author cites 9:67 and 2:44 for nasiya meaning abandonment, and an unnamed poet who uses nāsiyan for leaving off spear thrusts in battle. TABRISI reporting ابن عباس وقتادة ومجاهد والربيع والسدي: One explanation asks God not to impose a duty people cannot carry out or punish them for abandoning or violating it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن الأنباري: Ibn al-Anbari takes forgetting here as deliberate neglect, since involuntary forgetfulness is already exempt from sin; he likewise takes error here as intentional, though the word can also mean inadvertence. RAZI-FULL: Al-Razi counts four kinds of supplication: the first three begin with “Our Lord,” while the fourth omits that vocative. RAZI-FULL: Al-Razi answers that forgetfulness may be culpable when someone neglects precautions, but excusable when warning signs were absent or the person took reasonable care; he gives examples involving impurity, mistaken shooting, and forgetting memorized Qurʾan. RAZI-FULL: Although neglecting precautions may be culpable, the person is then punished for deliberately failing to take care, not for the lapse itself; the verse therefore still supports hope of pardon for grave sinners. RAZI-FULL: A second sense of forgetfulness is abandonment, supported by Qurʾanic usage at 20:115 and 9:67. RAZI-FULL: On the abandonment reading, error means doing an act on the basis of a mistaken interpretation. RAZI-FULL: The fourth prayer omits “Our Lord” because a call is needed at a distance; its omission signals that persistent entreaty brings the servant near to God. QURTUBI-FULL reporting قيل: A report says sincere raiders who leave home beating drums cast fear among unbelievers for a month, whether or not the enemy knows they have departed; the verses were revealed after the Prophet returned. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الزمخشري: Zamakhshari likewise supplies an omitted verb, “we seek Your forgiveness and do not deny You,” making the clause declarative. Against: ABUHAYYAN-FULL: He finds the omitted-relative analysis weak because the deleted relative has no preceding relative to license its omission; Ḥassān's verse has a repeated من as its antecedent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قطرب، والطبري: Quṭrub and al-Ṭabarī gloss نسينا as “we left/omitted”; the source then begins their gloss of وأخطأنا.
